title: The delivery framework (prompt to deep dives)
scopeHtml:
Scope: six-step framework: requirements, estimation, API and data, high-level design, deep dives, wrap-up.

Scope: six-step framework: requirements, estimation, API and data, high-level design, deep dives, wrap-up.

notes.title: Why use a framework
notes.html:
A framework is a fixed order of steps that stops you forgetting things when nervous. Under pressure, people jump to their favourite database. A framework makes you gather requirements first, so the design answers the actual question.

The one used throughout these notes has six steps: requirements, estimation, API and data model, high-level design, deep dives, wrap-up.

Worked example. Without a framework, a candidate asked to "design Dropbox" spends 25 minutes on file chunking and never mentions sharing, sync conflicts or storage cost. With the framework, step 1 surfaces "sync across devices" and "share links", step 2 shows 500M users x 2 GB = 1 EB of raw data (so dedup and tiering matter), and the deep dive is picked deliberately.

Industry examples. This mirrors how real design docs at Google and Amazon are structured: goals and non-goals, scale, API, design, alternatives, risks. Amazon's "6-pager" and Google's design docs both force a requirements-first order.

Everyday analogy. A pilot's checklist: boring, but the reason planes stay up.

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting the framework like a script; adapt the time to what the interviewer cares about.
  • Skipping a step because "it is obvious".

notes.title: Step 1: requirements
notes.html:
Ask what the system must do (functional) and how well it must do it (non-functional). Limit to the core 3 to 5 features and say what is out of scope.

Functional examples for a ride-hailing app: request a ride, see driver location, pay. Non-functional: latency of matching under 2 s, 99.95% availability, strong consistency for payments, eventual for location.

Questions that unlock the design:

  • How many users, and daily active?
  • Read-heavy or write-heavy?
  • Is stale data acceptable? For how long?
  • Global or one region?
  • Any compliance (PCI, GDPR)?

Decision gravity. The scope you agree on is reversible during the interview but expensive in real life: dropping "edit message" at day one is easy, adding it later changes the schema and the sync protocol. State assumptions so the interviewer can correct you.

Industry examples. WhatsApp chose to be a messaging-first product with delivery guarantees but no server-side history for years; that non-functional decision shaped its Erlang design. Stripe puts correctness and idempotency above raw latency for money movement.

Everyday analogy. A tailor measures before cutting cloth.

Common interview traps.

  • Asking twenty questions; pick the ones that change the design.
  • Leaving non-functional requirements out; they pick the database and replication.

notes.title: Step 2: estimation
notes.html:
Turn users into requests per second, storage and bandwidth in two minutes, to see which part is hard. Full technique is in the next note (F3). The point here is to use the numbers.

Quick pattern: DAU x actions per day / 86,400 = average QPS; peak is about 2x to 3x. Storage = items per day x size x retention. Bandwidth = QPS x payload.

Worked example. 20M DAU, 10 reads and 1 write per user per day. Reads: 200M/day = 2,300/s, peak 7,000/s. Writes: 20M/day = 230/s. One Postgres primary handles 230 writes/s trivially, and 7,000 reads/s is cache or replica territory, not sharding territory. The estimate has just saved you from over-engineering.

Industry examples. Instagram early on ran on a few Postgres instances; numbers told them sharding by user ID could wait.

Everyday analogy. Counting guests before ordering food.

Common interview traps.

  • Stating numbers and then never using them.
  • False precision; round to one significant figure.

notes.title: Step 3: API and data model
notes.html:
Define the few endpoints that carry the main flows, and the core tables or documents. This pins down what moves between boxes.

POST /v1/rides
{ "pickup": {"lat": 12.97, "lng": 77.59}, "dropoff": {"lat": 12.93, "lng": 77.62}, "idempotency_key": "9f2c..." }

Data model sketch for rides: rides(id, rider_id, driver_id, status, fare, created_at), driver_locations(driver_id, lat, lng, ts). Note which side needs the index and which access patterns you will serve ("rides for a rider, newest first").

Decision gravity. A public API is a one-way door: once clients depend on a field, you cannot remove it. A database schema is semi-reversible with migrations (expensive at scale). Version APIs (/v1) and prefer additive changes.

Industry examples. Stripe's API versioning by date and idempotency keys is the textbook example. Twitter moved from API v1.1 to v2 with years of overlap.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant menu: customers order from it, so changing a dish name affects everyone.

Common interview traps.

  • Designing 30 endpoints; show the 3 to 5 that matter.
  • Forgetting pagination and idempotency on write endpoints.
  • Choosing a schema before stating the access patterns.

notes.title: Step 4: high-level design
notes.html:
Draw the simplest design that meets the requirements, then trace the main request through it. Start with client, load balancer, stateless service, database. Add a cache, queue or CDN only when a number or requirement justifies it.

Walk one write and one read through the picture out loud: "the client posts, the service validates, writes to the DB, publishes an event; the read goes to cache first".

Worked example. Photo upload: client gets a pre-signed S3 URL (so a 5 MB image never passes through app servers), uploads directly, then calls the service with the object key. This keeps 1,000 uploads/s x 5 MB = 5 GB/s off your app tier.

Industry examples. Instagram and Dropbox use pre-signed or direct-to-storage uploads. Netflix places video behind its own CDN (Open Connect appliances) because video bandwidth dwarfs everything else.

Decision gravity. Adding a component is easy to draw and expensive to operate: every box needs monitoring, on-call and a failure story. Start small, add with justification.

Everyday analogy. Sketching the floor plan before furnishing rooms.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing every possible component in the first five minutes.
  • Boxes without arrows labelled by protocol or data.

notes.title: Step 5: deep dives
notes.html:
Pick the one or two hardest parts and go down to mechanism. Usually the interviewer steers; if not, propose: "the interesting problems here are X and Y, which one first?"

Common deep-dive topics: sharding key and hot partitions, cache invalidation, ordering and exactly-once, fan-out on write vs read, idempotency, rate limiting, consistency between services.

Worked example. Feed fan-out: a user with 300 followers posting triggers 300 timeline writes, fine. A celebrity with 50M followers would trigger 50M writes per post, so use a hybrid: fan out on write for normal users, merge celebrity posts at read time.

Industry examples. Twitter documented exactly this hybrid for timelines. Instagram and Facebook use ranking at read time on top of candidate lists.

Decision gravity. Fan-out strategy is a one-way-ish door: switching changes storage layout and latency profile. State the threshold (for example 100K followers) and that it is tunable.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper: print and deliver to every house (write) versus keep a stack at the shop (read).

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing a topic you cannot go deep on; pick one you know.
  • Reciting a technology feature list instead of the mechanism.

notes.title: Step 6: wrap-up and trade-offs
notes.html:
Reserve the last 5 minutes to list bottlenecks, failure modes, monitoring and what you would build next. This is where senior candidates stand out.

Checklist:

  • Single points of failure and how you remove them.
  • What happens when the DB, cache or queue is down?
  • Metrics and alerts: p99 latency, error rate, queue lag, replication lag.
  • Cost: biggest line item and how to cut it.
  • Evolution: what changes at 10x load.

Worked example. "If Redis dies, reads fall back to Postgres at 7,000/s, which one replica can take (about 10K simple reads/s), but I would add a circuit breaker and rate limit so the DB is not flattened by a cache stampede."

Industry examples. Facebook's 2010 and later outages from cache or config failures are classic stories on thundering herd; Netflix's chaos engineering practice exists to test these answers.

Everyday analogy. Reading the checklist before leaving the house: stove off, keys, wallet.

Common interview traps.

  • Running out of time and skipping this entirely.
  • Saying "it is fine" without a number or mechanism.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Use a fixed order: requirements, estimation, API and data, high-level, deep dives, wrap-up.
  • Requirements: few core features, explicit non-functional goals, state assumptions.
  • Numbers must change the design; stop if they say "one box is enough".
  • API and schema are the contract; public APIs are one-way doors.
  • Start simple, add components with a reason; trace one read and one write.
  • Go deep on one or two hard parts; finish with failures, monitoring, cost, 10x.

questions.promptHtml: Why should you follow a fixed framework in a design interview, and what are its steps?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether the candidate has a repeatable process under pressure, and whether they treat it as a tool, not a script.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A framework is a fixed order that stops me forgetting things when nervous. Mine has six steps: requirements, estimation, API and data model, high-level design, deep dives, wrap-up. It forces requirements before my favourite database, so the design answers the real question. I adapt the time to what the interviewer cares about.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Requirements -> Estimation -> API and data -> High-level -> Deep dives -> Wrap-up

Without it, "design Dropbox" turns into 25 minutes on file chunking and never mentions sharing, sync conflicts or storage cost. With it, step 1 surfaces sync and share links, step 2 shows 500M users x 2 GB = 1 EB raw, so dedup and tiering matter, and the deep dive is chosen deliberately. The same order is used in real design docs: goals and non-goals, scale, API, design, alternatives, risks.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reciting it like a script even when the interviewer steers elsewhere.
  • Skipping a step because "it is obvious".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the interviewer jumps to a deep dive at minute 5? -> Follow, and fill earlier steps briefly where they affect the answer.
  2. Which step do people skip most? -> Wrap-up and estimation.
  3. How is this like a design doc? -> Goals and non-goals, scale, API, design, alternatives, risks; the order forces requirements first.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: lists steps. Senior: explains the failure it prevents and adapts it live.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Design docs without non-goals are where scope creep starts; the framework is the same habit.

questions.promptHtml: What do you ask in the requirements step, and why do non-functional requirements matter so much?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Non-functional requirements choose the database, replication and consistency model; candidates who skip them design the wrong system.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I separate functional (what the system does, core 3 to 5 features, with explicit out-of-scope) from non-functional (how well: latency, availability, consistency, scale, compliance). Non-functional ones decide storage and replication. For ride-hailing: matching in under 2 s, 99.95% availability, strong consistency for payments, eventual for driver location.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Questions that change the design:

  • DAU and total users?
  • Read-heavy or write-heavy?
  • Is stale data acceptable, and for how long?
  • Global or single region?
  • Compliance (PCI, GDPR)?
Prompt -> Functional (what)     \
                                 -> Scope agreed
Prompt -> Non-functional (how well) /

The agreed scope is reversible within the interview but expensive in real life: dropping "edit message" on day one is easy; adding it later changes the schema and the sync protocol. State assumptions so the interviewer can correct them.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Asking twenty questions; ask those that change the design.
  • Leaving non-functional requirements out.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which question is the most valuable? -> Read/write ratio and consistency tolerance; they pick caching and storage.
  2. Why state out-of-scope? -> Protects the time budget and shows scoping judgement.
  3. How do compliance needs change design? -> Data residency, encryption, audit logs and retention constrain region layout and storage.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: lists features. Senior: ties each non-functional goal to a design consequence and states the one-way-door cost of scope.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Projects that never wrote "stale up to 5 s is fine" later paid for strong consistency they did not need.

questions.contextHtml: Prompt: "Design a food delivery app like Swiggy." You have 4 minutes for requirements. You can think of about 25 questions: payment methods, languages, dark mode, restaurant onboarding, coupons, ratings, live tracking, scheduling, refunds, surge pricing, and more.
questions.promptHtml: Which questions do you ask, and what do you declare out of scope?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Asks all 25 or asks none. Neither shows judgement about what changes the design.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (a) Core flow: browse, order, pay, track? (b) Scale: DAU and orders per day, and the peak (lunch and dinner)? (c) Live tracking freshness: location every 5 s? (d) Consistency: order and payment strongly consistent; menu and location eventual? (e) One country or multi-region?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Write the 4 in-scope flows and 5 out-of-scope items (coupons, ratings, scheduling, restaurant onboarding, refunds).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Design drivers: peak order burst, live tracking write volume, inventory consistency.
  4. How I'd verify each: Quick numbers: 5M orders/day = about 58/s average, peak 10x in the lunch window is about 600/s; 200K active drivers x one ping per 5 s = 40,000 location writes/s, which is the bigger load.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable; the requirements show the hard part is location ingestion, not orders.
  6. Fix: Carry the scope into API and data model; mention that I will revisit refunds if time allows.
  7. Prevention: Keep a short "assumptions" corner of the board.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not ask about dark mode or languages; they do not change the architecture.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Interviewer says "include surge pricing" -> add a pricing service reading demand per zone; I would state it costs a new data pipeline and drop something else.
  • "Strong consistency everywhere" -> I push back with the cost: availability and latency for tracking where staleness is harmless.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a candidate who found location writes (40,000/s) were 70x the order rate spent the deep dive there and was rated top of the loop.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: starts designing without questions.
  • Hire: 4 to 5 relevant questions and a stated scope.
  • Strong hire: uses the answers to identify the dominant load before drawing.

questions.promptHtml: Why do you define the API and data model before the architecture, and which parts are hard to change later?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests contract thinking and awareness of one-way doors.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The API and schema pin down what moves between boxes and which access patterns I must serve. A public API is a one-way door: once clients rely on a field I cannot remove it, so I version (/v1) and prefer additive changes. A schema is semi-reversible but migrations at scale are expensive. I list access patterns first and then choose keys and indexes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
POST /v1/rides
{ "pickup": {"lat": 12.97, "lng": 77.59}, "dropoff": {"lat": 12.93, "lng": 77.62}, "idempotency_key": "9f2c..." }

Data sketch: rides(id, rider_id, driver_id, status, fare, created_at) and driver_locations(driver_id, lat, lng, ts). Access pattern "rides for a rider, newest first" implies an index on (rider_id, created_at desc). Write endpoints need idempotency keys; list endpoints need pagination (cursor, not offset, at scale).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• 30 endpoints; show the 3 to 5 that matter.
  • No pagination or idempotency on write endpoints.
  • Choosing a schema before stating access patterns.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why an idempotency key? -> Client retries on timeout would otherwise create two rides or charges.
  2. Cursor vs offset pagination? -> Offset scans and skips rows (slow and unstable under inserts); a cursor seeks on an index.
  3. How would you evolve a public API? -> Additive fields, new version for breaking changes, long overlap period, usage telemetry before removal.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: lists endpoints and tables. Senior: ties them to access patterns and names which decisions are irreversible.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A field name shipped in a mobile app cannot be changed until the old app versions die, which can take years.

questions.contextHtml: Prompt: an internal news-feed for an enterprise app. 20M DAU, each user does 10 reads and 1 write per day. The candidate before you proposed sharding by user ID, Kafka and Cassandra. You are asked to do the estimate and choose storage.
questions.promptHtml: Do the numbers and say what they imply.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Computes the numbers and then ignores them: "so we shard".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Peak factor? Payload size? Staleness tolerance? (Assume 3x peak, 2 KB per item, a few seconds stale is fine.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I compute first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Reads are 10x writes; one primary may suffice for writes; reads need a cache or replicas.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reads: 20M x 10 = 200M/day = about 2,300/s, peak about 7,000/s. Writes: 20M/day = about 230/s, peak about 700/s. Storage: 20M x 2 KB = 40 GB/day, 14.6 TB/year before replication.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable.
  6. Fix: One Postgres primary handles 230 writes/s trivially; 7,000 reads/s is cache or one or two replicas (about 10K simple reads/s each, verify with a load test). Storage grows 14.6 TB/year, so plan partitioning by time and archiving, not user sharding yet.
  7. Prevention: State the trigger: shard when writes exceed what one primary sustains, or data exceeds a node.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use Cassandra and Kafka; an extra system adds operations with no number that justifies it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• DAU grows 10x -> writes 2,300/s, reads 23,000/s; still one primary plus replicas and cache, but start planning the partition key.
  • Cache hit ratio 90% -> DB sees about 700 reads/s at peak; replicas are barely needed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: early photo-sharing style apps ran for years on a few Postgres instances because the arithmetic said sharding could wait.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: numbers unused.
  • Hire: numbers lead to a simple design.
  • Strong hire: also gives the storage growth, the scale trigger and the load-test caveat.

questions.contextHtml: Photo upload for a social app: 1,000 uploads/s at peak, 5 MB per image. Your first draft routes uploads through the app servers to a database. App servers show 90% CPU and network saturation, and upload p99 is 12 s.
questions.promptHtml: Redraw the upload path and justify each box.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more app servers and a bigger database." Keeps 5 GB/s of blob traffic flowing through the stateless tier.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Max file size? Need virus or content scanning? Must the image be visible immediately after upload?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap upload concurrency and file size at the gateway to protect the app tier.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) blobs pass through app servers; (2) blobs are stored in a DB; (3) synchronous processing (thumbnails) inline.
  4. How I'd verify each: Bandwidth: 1,000 x 5 MB = 5 GB/s through the app tier, about 40 Gbps; check NIC metrics, DB row sizes, and request timing breakdown.
  5. Root cause: Large payloads travel through compute that only needs to authorise and record metadata.
  6. Fix: Client asks the service for a pre-signed URL; uploads straight to object storage; then calls the service with the object key to create the metadata row; an event triggers async thumbnail generation via a queue and workers; CDN serves reads.
Client -> App service: request upload URL
Client -> Object store: PUT image (pre-signed)
Client -> App service: confirm(key)
App service -> Queue -> Worker -> Object store (thumbnails)
  1. Prevention: Alert on app-tier egress and upload p99; lifecycle rules for abandoned uploads.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not scan inline on the request path; I would mark the post "processing" until the worker finishes. The pre-signed URL expiry is a security setting to keep short.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Client confirms but never uploaded -> confirm step does a HEAD on the object; the metadata row stays pending.
  • Resume a flaky mobile upload -> multipart or resumable upload; verify the storage API supports it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: moving uploads to direct-to-storage dropped app-tier CPU by about 80% in one release without adding any servers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale up the same path.
  • Hire: pre-signed direct upload plus async processing.
  • Strong hire: numbers, confirm and abandoned-upload handling, security and CDN.

questions.contextHtml:
A candidate proposes this payments-style API in an interview:

POST /createPayment            body: {userId, amount, currency}
GET  /getPayments?page=3&size=50&userId=42
DELETE /payment/17             (removes the record)
Response: {"status":"ok","amount":12.34}

The mobile client retries on timeout. Support reports duplicate charges and slow listing for users with 100K payments.
questions.promptHtml: List the design flaws and fix the contract.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only renames endpoints to REST style. Misses idempotency, money representation and pagination.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the API public (one-way door)? Do clients retry automatically? Which currencies? Is deletion legally allowed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a server-side dedupe on (userId, client request hash) to stop duplicate charges while the new contract is built.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) no idempotency key, so retries double-charge; (b) offset pagination degrades with depth (page=3 is fine, page=2000 scans 100K rows); (c) amount as a float; (d) DELETE loses financial records; (e) no version; (f) userId in query string rather than derived from auth.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay a timeout in a test; EXPLAIN the list query at deep offsets; check the stored amount type.
  5. Root cause: The contract was designed before failure and access patterns.
  6. Fix:
POST /v1/payments          header: Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
                           body: {amount_minor: 1234, currency: "INR"}
GET  /v1/payments?limit=50&cursor=<opaque>      (user from auth token)
POST /v1/payments/17/refunds                    (no delete; append-only)

Amounts as integer minor units; cursor on (created_at, id); response includes id and status. 7. Prevention: API review checklist: idempotency, pagination, versioning, error model, auth. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not keep the old fields forever without a deprecation date; but I would not remove them without telemetry, because a public API is a one-way door.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same key, different body -> return 422 or 409; keys must be bound to the request payload.
  • How long do you keep idempotency keys? -> Longer than the longest client retry window (for example 24 h); verify against the business rule.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a float amount rounded 0.1 + 0.2 style errors into reconciliation breaks of a few paise per thousand transactions, found only at month end.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cosmetic REST fixes.
  • Hire: idempotency, cursor pagination, money type.
  • Strong hire: also versioning, append-only refunds, key-payload binding and key retention.

questions.promptHtml: How do you choose what to deep dive on, and what does a good deep dive look like? Use feed fan-out as the example.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Depth separates senior from mid; they want to see whether you can pick a hard part and explain the mechanism and its threshold.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I pick the one or two hardest parts and go to mechanism, usually steered by the interviewer; if not, I propose: "the interesting problems are X and Y, which first?" For feeds the choice is fan-out on write versus on read. Normal users fan out on write; celebrities are merged at read time. I state the threshold and that it is tunable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Typical deep dives: sharding key and hot partitions, cache invalidation, ordering and exactly-once, fan-out, idempotency, rate limiting, consistency between services.

Post -> Fan-out service -> (Follower timeline caches)   [skip celebrities]
Reader -> timeline cache + celebrity posts merged at read time

A user with 300 followers: 300 timeline writes per post, fine. A celebrity with 50M followers: 50M writes per post, not fine. Hybrid: write for normal users, read-merge for users above a threshold (for example 100K followers). Switching strategy later changes the storage layout and the latency profile, so it is a one-way-ish door.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing a topic you cannot go deep on.
  • Reciting a feature list instead of the mechanism.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the timeline cache store? -> Lists of post IDs, not whole posts; hydrate from a post store.
  2. What happens when a user crosses the threshold? -> Backfill or let old entries age; double-run briefly; define a hysteresis.
  3. How do you rank? -> Candidate list from cache, ranked at read time by a ranking service.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Mid: "use fan-out on write". Senior: shows the arithmetic that breaks it, the hybrid, the threshold, and the migration cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A single celebrity post once caused a multi-minute write backlog in a naive push-only feed (a composite pattern, widely documented).

questions.contextHtml:
Your push-based feed has run fine for a year. A user with 8M followers posts. Within 2 minutes:

fanout_queue_depth        0 -> 6,400,000
fanout_worker_lag_s       2 -> 540
timeline_cache_write_qps  25,000 -> 180,000 (cache CPU 95%)
feed_read_p99_ms          120 -> 2,300  (all users)

Median users post 0.5 per day. A deploy happened 3 hours ago (red herring: it only changed image sizes).
questions.promptHtml: Stop the damage and fix the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more workers and cache nodes." Scales the symptom and still hurts everyone's reads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it one post or a pattern? Is the cache shared with reads? Are workers prioritised? When did the 8M account last post?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause or throttle fan-out for that author; drain their job into a separate low-priority queue; protect the read path (reads must not share the saturated cache CPU).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) celebrity author on push path (matches 8M jobs); (b) retry storm doubling writes; (c) the deploy (unlikely, change unrelated).
  4. How I'd verify each: Group queue messages by author id; check retry counters; compare traffic before and after the deploy.
  5. Root cause: Fan-out cost scales with followers: 8M writes per post, shared queue and cache with everyone else, no cap.
  6. Fix: Short term: mark the account "pull" and exclude it from fan-out, merge its posts at read time. Long term: hybrid threshold (for example 100K followers), separate queues by tier, per-author rate cap, separate cache for celebrity posts.
  7. Prevention: Alert on fan-out per post, queue age, and per-author job count; load test with a synthetic 10M follower post.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just scale cache; read-time merging adds read latency and cost for readers following many celebrities, which I accept and bound with a cap on how many celebrity feeds merge per request.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The celebrity unfollow storm? -> Deletions are cheap if the cache is per-user lists; rate-limit and batch.
  • Post edit or delete after fan-out -> only the post store changes; timelines hold IDs so hydration shows the update.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a high-profile account's post delayed ordinary users' feeds by minutes because both shared one worker pool; priority queues were the quickest fix.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale-up only.
  • Hire: isolates the celebrity case and proposes hybrid.
  • Strong hire: also protects reads, tiers queues, adds alerts and a load test.

questions.contextHtml:
In your wrap-up you said "if Redis dies, reads fall back to Postgres". The interviewer asks you to walk that through at 7,000 reads/s peak. One Postgres replica handles about 10K simple reads/s but your fallback queries are heavier joins. Redis restarts at 3 pm.

redis_up                      1 -> 0 (3:00) -> 1 (3:04)
cache_hit_ratio               96% -> 0% -> 12%
pg_replica_cpu                20% -> 100%
pg_active_connections         80 -> 500 (max_connections 500)
api_error_rate                0.1% -> 38%
questions.promptHtml: What happens, and what do you build so it does not?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It falls back and it is fine." No number, no mechanism, and it ignores that a cold cache and heavy queries make it a stampede.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Query cost in the fallback? Are keys all expiring at once? Is there request coalescing?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load: rate limit, serve stale or reduced responses, open a circuit breaker so the DB is not flattened.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) cache stampede on a cold cache; (b) connection pool exhaustion at 500; (c) heavier fallback queries than assumed.
  4. How I'd verify each: DB pg_stat_activity and top queries; ratio of identical concurrent queries; replica CPU.
  5. Root cause: After a restart every request misses; 7,000/s of heavy reads reach a replica sized for simple ones, and identical misses are not collapsed.
  6. Fix: Request coalescing (single-flight) per key; jittered TTLs; warm the cache before taking traffic; replicated Redis with automatic failover; circuit breaker and fallback to degraded content; capacity for the DB at the cache-cold load or a limit that protects it.
  7. Prevention: Game day: kill the cache in staging under load; alert on hit ratio drops and connection counts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not oversize the DB for the cold-cache worst case (costly); I accept degraded responses for a few minutes instead.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just a larger pool? -> More connections makes the DB slower; use a pooler and bound concurrency.
  • Is serving stale OK? -> For feeds yes; for balances no; requirements decide.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a cache failover caused a 20 minute outage because every miss ran a 200 ms query; single-flight alone cut DB load by about 90%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "fall back to DB".
  • Hire: names stampede, breaker and TTL jitter.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the fallback load, coalescing, warm-up, degraded mode and a game day.

questions.contextHtml: It is minute 41 of 45. You finished a deep dive and the interviewer says "any last thoughts?" You have designed a booking system for 5M DAU: gateway, booking service, Postgres primary with 2 replicas, Redis cache, a queue for notifications.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "I think that is it" or a half-finished extra detail. No failure modes, monitoring, cost or evolution.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: None; I announce a structured close: "failures, monitoring, cost, then 10x".
  2. Immediate mitigation: Start with the single points of failure: primary (promote a replica, plan RPO/RTO), Redis (fallback with breaker), queue (outbox table).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Most likely incident sources: replication lag on replica reads after a write, cache stampede, queue backlog.
  4. How I'd verify each: Metrics and alerts: p99 latency, error rate, replication lag, queue age, cache hit ratio.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable.
  6. Fix: Cost: the biggest line is probably DB and egress; reserve instances and cache hot reads. At 10x: shard by hotel or region, split the read path.
  7. Prevention: Runbooks, game days, SLOs with burn-rate alerts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not introduce new components now; I would state what I would build next and why.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Which risk worries you most? -> Double-booking under concurrent writes; I would use a unique constraint or row lock on the inventory row.
  • What would you cut if the deadline halves? -> The cache and queue; Postgres alone handles the estimated load.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: two equally strong designs; the one with a 3-minute failure and cost wrap-up was rated higher because "operations" had a signal.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no wrap-up.
  • Hire: SPOFs, metrics, one cost or scale remark.
  • Strong hire: all four (failures, monitoring, cost, 10x) with numbers and a prioritised risk.

questions.contextHtml: Prompt: "Design Dropbox." Assumptions you gather: 500M users, average 2 GB each, 20% daily active, devices sync automatically, sharing by link, version history. The interviewer says "we have 35 minutes and I care about cost and correctness".
questions.promptHtml: Run the framework and say where you would spend the deep dive.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Spends all time on chunking the file upload and never mentions storage cost, sync conflicts or sharing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Max file size? Conflict policy (last writer wins or keep both)? Versions retained how long? Dedup across users allowed (privacy)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the scope: upload, download, sync, share link, versions; out: real-time collaborative editing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cost and correctness drivers: raw storage, dedup and tiering, sync conflicts, metadata consistency.
  4. How I'd verify each: 500M x 2 GB = 1 EB raw (10^18 B); x3 replicas = 3 EB, or about 1.5 EB with erasure coding. Daily active 100M users; if each changes 50 MB per day that is 5 PB/day of changes, so chunking and dedup are required.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable.
  6. Fix: Split files into chunks (for example 4 MB, verify), content-hash each chunk, upload only missing chunks; metadata DB (strongly consistent) maps file to chunk list and version; blobs in object storage with tiering of cold data; sync via change feed or long polling with cursors; conflict creates a "conflicted copy".
  7. Prevention: Monitor dedup ratio, storage growth, sync latency, metadata DB replication lag.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Cross-user dedup saves space but leaks "does this file exist" information; I would restrict it or use convergent encryption with care. I would not use eventual consistency for the chunk-list metadata.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two devices edit offline -> conflicted copy, not silent overwrite; version vector or server revision check.
  • Large file upload fails at 99% -> chunk-level resume.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a storage company reached profitability only after moving cold data to erasure coding, because raw replication cost dominated its bill.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only chunking, no cost.
  • Hire: framework applied, dedup and metadata split.
  • Strong hire: EB-scale arithmetic, conflict policy, tiering, privacy trade-off and one-way-door awareness.
